findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and the problem it solves ("AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable"). A first-time reader can say what it is within seconds.
findings.source: header, first lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository."

findings.text: What to do next is easy to find. There is a link at the top, and the Next steps section lists the prerequisites (git 2.40+, a C linker, curl, Claude Code or npm), a clone command, `./setup.sh` and a first command, `athena ask "add a changelog"`.
findings.source: header: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and section "Next steps"

findings.text: This URL is Athena's home page, but almost all of the page studies a different project, firstmate. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena has to read past states, transitions, exit codes and 45 claims about firstmate. Those sections answer none of their questions about Athena.
findings.source: title "Athena explains how firstmate handles work" and lede "This page is that study of firstmate."

findings.text: The page never shows Athena's main output: a commit traced to the request, the models, the cost and the verdict. The demo is a different ability (reading a project), so the reader takes the core promise on trust.
findings.source: lede: "It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The lede says one model does the work and a different one checks it, but the install steps name only Claude Code. A newcomer can't tell which models or accounts they need, or what a run might cost.
findings.source: Next steps: "either Claude Code or npm (to install Claude Code)"

findings.text: This link speaks to an "owner" with pending proposals. A first-time visitor has no idea who that is, so it adds noise near the top of the page.
findings.source: header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The study itself is well built for a stranger. It gives a plain one-line definition, then a "Words used first" list before those terms appear, then one task followed from start to finish.
findings.source: Start here: "Firstmate is a tool that keeps a backlog of programming tasks and hands each one to a separate AI coding tool, called a worker"

findings.text: The same facts are repeated in Start here, the transition cards and the Glossary; the yolo rule appears at least five times. This makes an already long page longer without telling the reader anything new.
findings.source: Start here / States / Transitions / Glossary: yolo, red and in-scope are each defined in several places

findings.text: The Counters section says t9 (ready → reopened) changes places-held, but the t9 card never mentions freeing a place. A careful reader can't check this link against the card.
findings.source: Counters: "places-held, changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11"

findings.text: The page says plainly that nothing was run and that claims come from reading the source. This candour helps the reader judge how far to trust the study.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read"
